back: Dry run -- shows the proposed diff without making any changes to real infrastructure.
Actually executes the changes shown by plan, prompting for confirmation by default.
Downloads providers and sets up the backend. Re-run whenever those change, not for every routine plan/apply.
JSON mapping of your config to real resource IDs. Can contain plaintext secrets -- never commit it to source control.
Shared, lockable state (e.g. S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud) -- prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state.
<resource_type>.<local_name>.<attribute> -- e.g. aws_instance.web.id, not just 'web.id'.
Read-only lookup of existing infrastructure. Terraform never creates, updates, or destroys what a data source reads.
-var/-var-file flag > *.auto.tfvars > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_ environment variable > default in the block.
Explicitly declares an ordering dependency when there's no implicit resource reference for Terraform's dependency graph to infer.
Declarative -- you describe the desired end state; Terraform's engine determines the steps to reach it.
The top-level configuration directory you run terraform commands from. Every config is technically a module.
Isolate state under one shared configuration/backend. Best when environments are structurally identical, differing only by input values.
When real infrastructure no longer matches state (e.g. a manual console change). terraform plan surfaces it by refreshing and diffing.
Associates an existing real resource with a resource block, writing state only -- in most versions you still write the matching config yourself.
Rewrites files to canonical style. Purely cosmetic, no behavior change -- often checked in CI.
Checks syntax and internal consistency locally, without contacting any backend or provider.
Forces a specific resource to be destroyed and recreated on the next apply -- the modern replacement for the old 'taint' command.
A data source that reads another configuration's outputs from its remote state -- the standard way to pass values between separately-applied root modules.
Child modules declare input variables, exactly like a root module -- that's the entire configuration mechanism for reuse.
Commonly cited around 70% on a scaled score -- confirm the current number with HashiCorp before registering.
